item.title: AUD/USD struggles to break key resistance despite hot Australia CPI and hawkish RBA
item.description:
Even with the latest developments out of Australia earlier today, AUD/USD is finding it tough to make any meaningful push higher. The pair continues to trade around 0.7030 on the day, once again knocking on the door of key technical resistance near its 100-day and 200-day moving averages.

The latest Australia CPI report was hotter than expected, with trimmed mean inflation rising to 3.7% against expectations of 3.6%. That certainly doesn't make the RBA's job any easier, especially with oil prices adding to inflation pressures.

And RBA governor Bullock didn't exactly mince her words either, warning that inflation remains "far too high". Her comments pretty much reinforces the narrative that the central bank is almost certainly poised for another rate hike next week, giving the aussie a fundamental reason to hold firmer. Or at least that is the case in theory.

But looking at the AUD/USD chart, buyers still have some convincing to do.

The double-bottom pattern near 0.6900 has set the pair up for a decent rebound in the past week or so, with the latest run up testing key resistance around 0.7030-50. And that is where the 100-day (red line) and 200-day (blue line) moving averages are starting to converge around. That makes for a rather stubborn technical hurdle, with buyers repeatedly struggling to establish a firm break above the region since last week.

A sustained push above the 200-day moving average at 0.7054 would be a more encouraging development, potentially opening the door towards 0.7100 before the descending trendline resistance closer to 0.7220 comes into focus next.

On the downside, the 0.7000 level remains the first key support to watch, followed by the 0.6900-0.6920 region and then the rising trendline support near 0.6900 as well.

So, what's next for the pair this week?

Well, the Fed could be one to have the bigger say in what happens next. A more hawkish message from Warsh & co. could give the dollar another lift, making it more difficult for AUD/USD to chase a break higher.

And with broader risk sentiment still looking fragile, particularly around tech stocks, the aussie might not exactly get much help from that side of the equation either. It all will depend on how big tech earnings play out later in the day, with watchful eyes on Microsoft and Alphabet earnings after the closing bell. That will also in turn have some potential spillover impact on how the bond market reacts.

In other words, there's still a lot to play for in broader markets for the second half of the week.

So even if the domestic story may be turning more supportive for the aussie, I wouldn't be convinced that AUD/USD can sustain the next leg higher until buyers can clear the resistance zone highlighted above.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Wall Street faces a double test as Fed decision and Microsoft, Alphabet earnings loom
item.description:
Wall Street enjoyed a bit of a breather in overnight trading, as the S&P 500 gained by 0.6% and Nasdaq closed higher by 1.2%. It's a welcome relief after drop in the past two weeks as tech shares bounced back, but there are still plenty of reasons for investors to be nervous in trading this week.

For one, the rebound overnight was not all too convincing once we start to dig a little deeper beneath the surface. It was largely driven by big tech names with most of the stocks in the S&P 500 actually closing lower. That's not a good signal on market breadth now, is it?

And with the Fed decision coming up later today, followed by earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet after the closing bell, there's still quite a lot that could go wrong.

Now, the Fed is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged. So, I don't see the decision itself being much of a surprise. All eyes will be on Fed chair Warsh's press conference as markets will be listening closely for any signals on December, particularly with Treasury yields still hovering near 5%.

With that in mind, any suggestion that policymakers are becoming even more uncomfortable with the inflation outlook could easily put another dent in risk sentiment.

And that will be especially relevant for tech stocks, where higher borrowing costs and lofty valuations are already making investors question just how much optimism is justified.

Microsoft's earnings will be closely scrutinised for whether its AI growth can continue to justify the enormous spending commitments. In particular, there will be plenty of watchful eyes on its Azure growth, cloud margins and capital expenditure especially.

As for Alphabet, they will face similar scrutiny with Google Cloud performance, AI monetisation and infrastructure spending all under the microscope.

At this point, I'm not sure that investors will be satisfied in just hearing that AI demand remains strong. It seems that they might want clearer evidence that all those billions being spent are translating into sustainable earnings growth. And that's where the real test for the AI trade lies at the moment.

It's going to be quite a tricky test for stocks and broader markets in the coming day(s). While a more hawkish Fed could put renewed upward pressure on Treasury yields, disappointing earnings guidance could reignite concerns over the AI spending boom. The latter is one that could even see both yields and stocks fall at the same time.

So while the calmer mood overnight is a little encouraging, it is best to be mindful that the real test for markets this week is still yet to come.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European markets brace for Fed decision as hot Australia CPI, RBNZ surprise and oil rally stir nerves
item.description:
It has been quite an eventful start to the day so far as the central bank bonanza rolls into town. That is putting inflation back in the spotlight with there already being plenty to digest before European traders get to their desks and before we even get to the main events later today.

To start with, we saw Australia's latest CPI report came in hotter than expected with trimmed mean inflation rising to 3.7%. That's not a good look and RBA governor Bullock was quick to respond in warning that inflation remains "far too high". The numbers certainly strengthen the argument for another rate hike, with Bullock's response underscoring the narrative that the central bank is facing an increasingly uncomfortable inflation outlook.

As such, that is now seeing markets step up their pricing for the next RBA meeting on 3 November, with traders pricing in roughly 76% odds of a 25 bps rate hike.

Meanwhile, the RBNZ delivered arguably the bigger surprise of the session after keeping its official cash rate unchanged at 2.75% in a narrow 4-3 vote. Markets had been expecting a 25 bps rate hike today, so the decision has definitely caught traders off guard and sent the kiwi sharply lower. NZD/USD is down 1.1% to 0.5615 on the day currently.

Having said that, the central bank hasn't abandoned its tightening bias altogether as the minority continued to take on a more hawkish stance. But at least for now, the shock of the decision is the one that will be reverberating as the RBNZ conviction doesn't look as strong as markets had thought coming into today.

Apart from central banks, oil prices are also back on the move following a reported Houthi attack on a major Saudi refinery. Adding to that, the US has also reportedly warned of a possible short but intense military campaign against Iran after the midterm elections. So, that is pushing oil prices higher with WTI crude nudging back above $101 on the day.

That's a lot to take in already and put together, they're not helping with the inflation narrative - especially when the bond market continues to be rather nervous this week, despite the recent pullback in yields.

10-year Treasury yields are still holding around 5.01%, so that is keeping borrowing costs and equity valuations firmly in focus. And higher oil prices will only serve to complicate that picture further, potentially making it harder for central banks to bring inflation under control.

As we head towards European morning trade, do keep a close watch on Treasury yields and the broader risk sentiment. However, the day ahead will be all about the main events tom come later in US trading mostly.

The Fed decision is the obvious headline event but big tech earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet will be just as important in shaping the market mood. With yields still elevated and investors questioning the returns on massive AI spending, big tech names don't have too much room in disappointing markets.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Topix explained: why Japan’s biggest-ever index overhaul will cull 683 stocks by 2028
item.description:
The immediate effect comes at Thursday’s close, when around $60 billion of passive trades is expected to cause sharp, short-lived price swings and heavy volume in affected stocks. That can briefly distort the Topix and individual names, which is why hedge funds have been positioning in advance. Over time, the quarterly weight cuts create steady selling pressure on smaller, less liquid companies and support larger stocks such as Kioxia. That may widen the gap between Japanese large caps and small caps. The 2027 re-evaluation gives companies a reason to improve liquidity and free float, which could encourage more unwinding of cross-shareholdings and buybacks. That fits the governance push foreign investors have rewarded. Watch for a temporary gap between the Topix and the Nikkei 225, which isn’t affected.

--- Japan is turning its sprawling Topix into a leaner, more investable benchmark, and with about ¥166 trillion tracking it, the reshuffle starts with a $60 billion trade on Thursday and keeps going for two years.

Summary:

  • The Topix’s largest-ever overhaul takes effect on October 30, with about $60 billion of passive trading expected at Thursday’s close, the Japan Times reported.
  • 683 companies that failed new liquidity and free-float tests will be phased out, with their weights cut in eight quarterly steps from January 2027 to zero in October 2028.
  • Companies that meet the criteria at an October 2027 re-evaluation stop being cut and remain in the index.
  • The index is projected to shrink from 1,669 members after October to about 986 by mid-2028.
  • About ¥166 trillion of passive assets track the Topix, per Daiwa, so index funds must sell dropped stocks and buy additions.
  • Kioxia’s weighting is set to rise, with hopes of around $13 billion of inflows, Bloomberg reported.

Japan’s main equity benchmark is undergoing the biggest overhaul in its history this week, with changes to the Topix index taking effect from Friday, October 30. Around $60 billion of passive trading is expected at Thursday’s close as index funds reposition, according to the Japan Times, and the reshuffle will continue to shape flows into Japanese stocks for the next two years.

The Topix, short for Tokyo Stock Price Index, has long been one of the broadest major equity benchmarks, covering a large share of companies listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. That breadth has drawn criticism, because it includes many small, thinly traded companies that are hard for large investors to buy. The Japan Exchange Group has been reforming the index to make it more investable, cutting the number of constituents from around 2,200 to around 1,700 in a first phase that ended in January 2025.

The second phase is far more ambitious. Under the periodic review published on October 7, stocks are now judged on annual trading value and on the market value of shares freely available to investors. Some 683 companies that failed to meet those tests will be phased out, while dozens of others have been added. Exchange data show the index had 1,636 members at the end of August and 1,669 after October’s changes, but the count is projected to fall to 986 once the transition is complete in mid-2028, plus any companies that requalify.

The phase-out is gradual by design. Rather than removing the 683 stocks at once, the exchange will cut their index weight in eight quarterly steps of 12.5 percentage points, starting in January 2027 and reaching zero in October 2028. Companies that meet the criteria at a re-evaluation in October 2027 will stop being cut and remain in the index. From October 2028, the Topix will be rebalanced annually.

The stakes are large because so much money tracks the index. Daiwa Securities estimates around ¥166 trillion of passive assets follow the Topix, including index funds and exchange-traded funds. When a stock’s weight is cut, those funds must sell it, and when a stock is added or up-weighted, they must buy, regardless of valuation. That mechanical demand is why hedge funds have been positioning ahead of the changes, the Japan Times reported, aiming to profit from price moves in affected stocks around the rebalancing.

Some well-known names stand to benefit. Memory chipmaker Kioxia is set to see its weighting rise, with hopes of around $13 billion of inflows, Bloomberg reported earlier this month. For the companies being phased out, the gradual schedule gives them time to lift trading liquidity or free float, through measures such as unwinding cross-shareholdings, in order to requalify.

Analysts see the reform as part of Tokyo’s wider push to improve corporate governance and valuations. Some argue that concentrating the benchmark in larger, more liquid companies could lift the market’s overall valuation and reinforce the long-running tilt toward large caps, while smaller companies dropped from the index could face weaker demand from passive investors.

For investors, the immediate focus is Thursday’s close, when the first rebalancing trades are expected. The longer-term effect will play out every quarter until 2028, making the overhaul a slow-moving but persistent force on Japanese equity flows.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Australia: Bullock and CPI build the case for a November hike Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock struck a hawkish tone at Senate Estimates, saying inflation is likely to run above the RBA’s August forecasts as the re-escalating Middle East conflict lifts energy prices and the labour market looks a little tighter than previously judged. After the data, she said inflation is far too high, that it is difficult to completely look through supply shocks and that domestic demand still exceeds supply, though she declined to give guidance on next week’s decision.

The September quarter CPI backed her concerns. The trimmed mean, the RBA’s main gauge of underlying inflation, rose 1.0% in the quarter and 3.7% year on year, above the 3.6% expected, while monthly headline inflation climbed to 4.3% in September. Together, the data and Bullock’s comments strengthen the case for a rate hike when the Board concludes its meeting on November 3.

New Zealand: a surprise hold, then hawkish guidance The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held its official cash rate at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote, defying around 90% market pricing for a hike and forecasts from all five major local banks. The majority, including Governor Anna Breman, cited lower-than-expected headline inflation of 3.7%, smaller pass-through from fuel and subdued wages, though all members agreed tighter policy is likely to be needed. At her press conference, Breman said further rate increases are likely at coming meetings and could extend into restrictive territory, and that a persistently weak New Zealand dollar could add to imported inflation.

FX: AUD/NZD jumps on policy divergence The New Zealand dollar fell sharply after the RBNZ decision, while the Australian dollar gained on the hotter CPI and Bullock’s comments. The diverging signals from the two central banks drove a strong rise in AUD/NZD.

Oil and geopolitics: supply risks return Oil prices rose, with Brent around $115 a barrel, after Yemen’s Houthis said they had struck Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery, a claim Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm. Geopolitical risk was reinforced by a Wall Street Journal report that the US has told several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a possible short, intense military campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, with President Donald Trump leaning toward a large strike but yet to decide. Market chatter also centred on the possibility of renewed Israeli strikes on Iran, although Israel’s defence minister has said there was no intention to attack before the election. Exit polls from Tuesday’s Israeli election pointed to no clear result, with official results due on November 4.

Equities: Kospi soars as SK Hynix delivers Asia-Pacific stocks followed Wall Street higher, where the Nasdaq outperformed. South Korea led the region, with the Kospi surging 6% and the Kosdaq up 3%, after SK Hynix reported a roughly sevenfold jump in third-quarter operating profit to around 83 trillion won, ahead of forecasts, as memory chip prices surged on AI demand. The chipmaker unveiled shareholder returns of about 100 trillion won, around $75 billion, for 2026, including more than 60 trillion won of share buybacks and cancellations and more than 30 trillion won in dividends, alongside a quarterly dividend of 20,000 won per share. Net profit missed forecasts, and the company said it expects DRAM demand to grow by a mid-20% rate in 2027. Elsewhere, Japan’s Nikkei rose 1.4%, China’s Shanghai Composite gained 0.5% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng added 0.2%.

Crypto policy: Bessent eyes agency route US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington can still deliver crypto regulation without new legislation. Speaking at Ripple’s Swell conference, he described the Senate’s failure to pass the Clarity Act as disappointing, but said Treasury would use its convening power to advance a regulatory framework through agency action with the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

item.title: RBNZ’s Breman: more hikes likely at coming meetings, possibly into restrictive territory
item.description:
Breman’s guidance partly reverses the dovish read of the hold. Signalling likely hikes at coming meetings, possibly into restrictive territory, should push December pricing back up, support front-end yields and help the New Zealand dollar recover some of its losses. Her explicit worry about a weak currency feeding imported inflation acts as a soft floor for the kiwi, since further falls make a hike more likely. Oil is the main swing factor: fuel is already lifting inflation toward 4.4%, so higher crude, especially if a US strike on Iran escalates after the midterms, would make a December hike much more likely. The guidance also narrows the policy gap with the RBA, which may cap AUD/NZD after this morning’s divergence.

---

The RBNZ held, then Breman spent the press conference telling markets not to read too much into it: more hikes are likely, and they may go further than planned.

Summary:

  • RBNZ Governor Anna Breman said further rate increases are likely at coming meetings, and tightening might be needed even into restrictive territory.
  • The committee agreed tighter policy is likely, conditional on the economy, and discussed whether rates could rise further than its projected OCR path.
  • Breman said the committee is concerned that a sustained fall in the NZ dollar could add to imported inflation.
  • She said the decision was based on the economic outlook, though the committee did look at market pricing, and that wage growth remains below levels consistent with the inflation target.
  • The committee discussed the risk of a correction in AI-related market assets.
  • Partial inflation indicators and labour data will be important ahead of the December Monetary Policy Statement.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Anna Breman said further interest rate increases are likely at coming meetings and could take policy into restrictive territory, sounding a more hawkish note at her media conference hours after the central bank surprised markets by holding its official cash rate at 2.75%.

Breman said the Monetary Policy Committee agreed that tighter policy is likely to be required, conditional on how the economy evolves. She said it is likely the RBNZ will deliver further rate increases at upcoming meetings, and that additional tightening might be needed even into restrictive territory, meaning rates high enough to actively slow the economy rather than simply removing stimulus. She also said the committee discussed whether rates could need to rise further than its existing projected path for the OCR.

The currency featured prominently. Breman said the committee discussed the decline in the New Zealand dollar and is concerned that, if the currency remains weak, it could add to imported inflation. The RBNZ’s statement noted that the trade-weighted exchange rate has fallen around 3% since early September, at a time when fuel prices have risen further because of disruptions in global energy markets.

Breman explained the decision to hold rather than hike in terms of the economic outlook, while acknowledging the committee did look at market pricing, which had priced roughly a 90% chance of a hike. She said conditions for returning inflation to target remain favourable, pointing to wage growth running below levels consistent with inflation at the 2% midpoint. That echoed the majority view in the committee’s 4-3 vote, which argued the two recent hikes give it time to assess their effects.

The governor also said the committee discussed the risk of a correction in AI-related market assets, building on the RBNZ’s warning that financial stability risks have increased because of high debt and opaque financing arrangements for some AI investment.

Looking ahead, Breman said partial inflation indicators and labour market data in the coming weeks will be important for the committee’s assessment. The next decision is due with the December Monetary Policy Statement, which will include updated forecasts and a new projected path for the OCR.

The press conference left markets with a mixed message: a decision that leaned dovish, and guidance from the governor that leaned hawkish. With a minority already pushing for a hike and Breman now signalling increases are likely, December is shaping up as a live meeting, particularly if fuel prices stay high and the currency remains weak. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US warns Gulf allies of possible short, intense Iran campaign after midterms: WSJ
item.description:
This is a direct upside risk for oil. A renewed US campaign against Iran would revive the threat of Iranian retaliation against Gulf energy facilities, shipping and infrastructure, which Iran has already shown it is willing to target. With Brent already around $115, the Houthi refinery claim adding to supply nerves and OPEC+ unlikely to add barrels on Sunday, a risk premium could build in the days before the November 3 midterms. Freight and insurance costs for Gulf shipping are also exposed. The inflation consequences extend well beyond the region: higher crude would add to the pressure that the RBA flagged today and complicate Fed policy. Safe-haven flows into the dollar are possible. Gold has tended to fall on escalation as rate expectations rise.

-- Washington is quietly telling Gulf allies to brace for a post-midterms strike on Iran, and with Tehran promising to hit back at energy targets, oil markets have six days to price the risk.

Summary:

  • The US told several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a possible short, intense military campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterms, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported.
  • Trump is leaning toward a large strike on Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites but has not decided, according to people familiar with his thinking.
  • The US is moving a Patriot system to the region, restocking munitions and adding a carrier strike group to roughly 20 warships already deployed. Israel has also prepared strike plans.
  • The White House declined to comment on military plans and said all options remain on the table to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon.
  • Iran has warned it would hit economic and civilian targets across the region, and retains hundreds to thousands of missiles.
  • Mediators are trying to revive talks, with little progress so far.

The United States has told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible short, intense military campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the conversations.

The warnings, delivered through diplomatic and military channels, are among a growing number of signs that the US and Israel are preparing for a new round of heavy combat operations aimed at degrading Iran’s capabilities and pushing Tehran toward negotiations, according to the Journal. President Donald Trump has not made a decision, but is leaning toward a large post-election attack that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, people familiar with his thinking told the newspaper. Trump has said he will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterms.

Military preparations are under way to give the president options. Officials told the Journal the US is moving a Patriot missile defence system from Texas to the region and has moved troops off bases where they were vulnerable. US forces have been restocking munitions, bomber and fighter aircraft are preparing for strikes, and an additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine expeditionary unit are poised to join roughly 20 other US warships in the Middle East next month. Israel has also prepared plans and targets for a new attack, the Journal reported, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continuing to push for a resumption of strikes.

The White House declined to comment on what it called sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, saying Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. Trump said at a rally last week that the US could carry out another limited version of the spring bombing campaign, known as Epic Fury, unless Iran agrees to a deal.

A return to airstrikes would mark a shift away from the administration’s economic pressure campaign, in which tighter sanctions and a naval blockade have cut off Iran’s oil sales for months. Several analysts quoted by the Journal questioned whether new strikes would succeed. One argued the US already holds a winning hand through sanctions and the blockade, while a former Israeli military intelligence official said further bombing could harden Tehran’s commitment to its missile and nuclear programmes rather than topple the government.

Iran has warned it would respond to any attack with strikes on economic and civilian targets across the region, as it did earlier in the war when it hit US bases, energy facilities and airports across the Gulf. It retains a stockpile of hundreds to thousands of missiles and is assembling new ballistic missiles from stockpiled parts, the Journal reported, while the US and its Gulf allies are still working to replenish missile defences depleted by earlier Iranian attacks.

Regional mediators are trying to revive talks to head off renewed fighting, but have so far made little progress, with Washington insisting on discussing Iran’s nuclear programme and Tehran setting tough conditions for resuming negotiations. With the midterms less than a week away, the window for diplomacy is narrowing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil edges higher after Houthis claim missile strike on Saudi Arabia’s biggest refinery
item.description:
The key issue for oil is whether the Houthi claim turns into confirmed lost supply. For now, the move reflects headline risk on a refinery Saudi Arabia hasn’t confirmed was hit, so prices are exposed to a reversal if the damage proves limited, or a sharper rally if refining capacity is knocked out. A hit to a facility of this size would matter more for refined products such as diesel than for crude, which fits the shipping and refining strains UBS and the RBNZ flagged this week. OPEC+ holding steady on Sunday, with most core members already below target, offers little cushion if supply is disrupted. Higher crude also feeds straight into the inflation concerns voiced today by RBA Governor Bullock (here and again here).

Oil clawed back some of Tuesday’s losses on a Houthi claim of a strike on Saudi Arabia’s biggest refinery, but until Riyadh confirms the damage, the market is pricing risk, not lost barrels.

Summary:

  • Brent rose around 1.3% to around $115 and WTI around 1.2% to around $101 as of 01:40 GMT, according to Reuters.
  • Yemen’s Houthis said they struck Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery, a 550,000 bpd facility. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike.
  • Reuters said the attack renewed concerns about Middle East supply risks. Prices had fallen nearly $2 on Tuesday as regional talks eased worries.
  • A Reuters poll pointed to a build of about 15,000 barrels in US crude inventories for the week ended October 23.
  • OPEC+ is expected to keep December output targets steady on Sunday, sources told Reuters, with most core members producing below target.
  • Russian crude exports from Baltic and Black Sea ports could fall next month as domestic refiners lift diesel output, traders said.

Oil prices rose in Asian trading on Wednesday after Yemen’s Houthis said they had struck Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery with a missile, a move Reuters said renewed concerns over Middle East supply risks linked to the conflict with Iran and its proxies.

Brent crude futures rose around 1.3% to around $115 a barrel as of 01:40 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude gained around 1.2% to around $101, according to Reuters. The move recovered part of Tuesday’s decline of nearly $2, when talks in the Middle East had helped ease supply worries.

The Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had hit the 550,000 barrel per day facility, intensifying their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest crude exporter and second-largest producer. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike, and there was no immediate information on any damage or disruption to operations. Reuters framed the price rise as a reaction to the attack reigniting supply concerns.

The gains came despite expectations of a small build in US crude inventories. A Reuters poll of eight analysts pointed to a rise of about 15,000 barrels in US crude stockpiles in the week ended October 23, a minimal change ahead of official data. 

Adding to the risk premium is speculation in markets that Israel could renew strikes on Iran following Tuesday’s general election. Exit polls suggested Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc fell well short of a 61-seat majority in most surveys, although official results are not due until November 4. Some commentators have suggested that an electoral setback could raise the risk of military escalation, and Israeli media reported before the vote that a plan to strike Iran had been discussed at senior levels. Israel’s defence minister dismissed reports of disagreement over such a plan as baseless and said there was no intention to attack Iran before the election, and there has been no official indication of imminent action. The chatter nonetheless helps explain why traders remain quick to price in Middle East supply risk.

Attention is also turning to OPEC+. The group is expected to keep its December output targets unchanged when it meets on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters, in line with market expectations. Production in most of the seven core members, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman, is running below their targets, which limits how much a decision on quotas changes actual supply.

Russian flows are another factor. Traders told Reuters that crude exports from Russia’s Baltic and Black Sea ports could fall next month as domestic refiners increase diesel production following a deal with Washington earlier this month.

The key question for prices is whether the strike causes any lasting loss of refining capacity. Until Saudi Arabia confirms the extent of any damage, the price reaction reflects risk rather than confirmed lost supply, leaving crude sensitive to further headlines from the region, Sunday’s OPEC+ meeting and this week’s US inventory data. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA’s Bullock: Inflation is far too high
item.description:
By saying it is hard to completely look through supply shocks, Bullock signalled that the RBA is less willing to ignore the energy-driven jump in prices than the RBNZ was earlier. Any further rise in crude therefore adds directly to the case for an RBA hike. Her blunt language (more here earlier), together with firmer core inflation and her view that demand still exceeds supply, supports pricing for a move on November 2 and 3, and backs the Australian dollar and front-end yields. The contrast with the RBNZ’s hold sharpens the policy divergence, which favours AUD/NZD. Bullock’s refusal to give guidance leaves some uncertainty, but the overall tone tilts clearly hawkish.

--- Bullock didn’t pre-announce a hike, but “far too high” and “difficult to look through supply shocks” are about as close as a central banker gets without saying it.

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Michele Bullock said inflation is far too high, in Senate committee testimony after the Q3 CPI release.
  • She said the data was consistent with upside inflation risks and that it is difficult to completely look through supply shocks.
  • Bullock said domestic demand is still higher than domestic supply, but declined to give guidance on the November 2 and 3 Board decision.
  • Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the CPI was in line with expectations but too high. Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said it was stronger than the RBA expected in August.
  • Hunter said she does not expect a recession in Australia.
  • The Q3 trimmed mean rose to 3.7% y/y, above the 3.6% expected, and September headline inflation hit 4.3%.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said inflation is far too high, as she and her senior colleagues responded to hotter-than-expected September quarter CPI data during a Senate committee hearing on Wednesday, days before the RBA Board meets to decide on interest rates.

Bullock said the latest figures were consistent with the upside risks to inflation the RBA had flagged, and that it is difficult to completely look through supply shocks such as the current surge in energy prices. She added that domestic demand is still running ahead of the economy’s capacity to supply it, a sign that price pressures are not only being imported. She declined, however, to give guidance on the Board’s decision on November 2 and 3.

Her deputy, Andrew Hauser, said the CPI numbers were in line with expectations but still too high, while Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said inflation came in stronger than the RBA had expected in August. The two comments are consistent: the data broadly matched what economists forecast ahead of the release, but ran above the path in the RBA’s August Statement on Monetary Policy. Hunter also said she does not expect Australia to fall into recession.

The remarks followed a data release that added to the RBA’s concerns. The trimmed mean, the central bank’s main gauge of underlying inflation, rose 1.0% in the September quarter and 3.7% year on year, above the 3.6% expected, while monthly headline inflation climbed to 4.3% in September. Earlier in the hearing, before the data was released, Bullock had said inflation was likely to run higher than the RBA’s August forecasts, citing re-escalating conflict in the Middle East, much higher energy prices and a labour market that looks a little tighter than the RBA had judged.

Bullock’s comment on supply shocks is significant. Central banks often look through one-off jumps in prices such as fuel, on the basis that they fade on their own. By saying that is hard to do completely, Bullock signalled that the RBA is concerned about higher energy costs spreading into broader prices and into inflation expectations, particularly with underlying inflation already above target.

The RBA has raised its cash rate by a cumulative 100 basis points this year. Bullock has said a key question for next week’s meeting is whether that tightening will be enough to return inflation to the 2% to 3% target in a reasonable time. While she stopped short of signalling a move, the combination of firmer core inflation, a tight labour market and the Governor’s blunt language keeps another hike firmly in play. The Board’s decision next week will be accompanied by updated forecasts. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUD/NZD in focus as hawkish RBA signals clash with RBNZ’s surprise 4-3 hold
item.description:
Both economies face the same fuel shock, but Bullock treats it as a reason for concern, while the RBNZ majority is betting weak demand will contain it. That difference in reaction is what drives the divergence. A widening gap in expected rates generally supports AUD/NZD, and a hike from the RBA next week, with the RBNZ waiting until December, would extend it. The main risk to the move is the RBNZ’s 4-3 split: hawkish signals from Breman at the press conference, or a firm December hike signal, could pull the cross back quickly. A softer tone from the RBA next week would do the same. Further gains in crude would test both banks, but the RBA currently looks the more willing to respond.

---

---

Within 90 minutes, Australia signalled it may need to tighten further and New Zealand decided to wait, and AUD/NZD is where that divergence shows up.

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Bullock said inflation will likely exceed the RBA’s August forecasts on higher energy prices and a tighter labour market, ahead of the November 2 and 3 meeting.
  • Australia’s Q3 trimmed mean rose to 3.7% y/y, above the 3.6% expected, and September headline inflation climbed to 4.3%.
  • The RBNZ held the OCR at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote, surprising markets and all five major NZ banks, which expected a hike.
  • The RBNZ said tighter policy is likely but conditional, with the next decision and new forecasts due in December.
  • Diverging rate expectations generally favour AUD/NZD, though the RBNZ’s split vote and its 4.4% December inflation forecast limit how far the gap can widen.
  • The next tests are Breman’s media conference at 02:00 GMT and the RBA decision next week.

Australia and New Zealand delivered sharply contrasting policy signals within 90 minutes on Wednesday, putting AUD/NZD in focus as a hawkish turn from the Reserve Bank of Australia met a surprise hold from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.

The Australian side leaned hawkish. RBA Governor Michele Bullock told a Senate committee that inflation is likely to run higher than the central bank forecast in August, citing a renewed surge in energy prices from the Middle East conflict and a labour market that looks a little tighter than previously judged. She said a key question for next week’s Board meeting is whether the 100 basis points of tightening delivered this year will be enough. Minutes later, September quarter data showed the RBA’s preferred trimmed mean inflation measure rising to 3.7% year on year, above the 3.6% expected, while monthly headline inflation climbed to 4.3% in September.

New Zealand went the other way. The RBNZ held its official cash rate at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote, against market pricing of around 90% for a hike and forecasts from all five major local banks. The majority, including Governor Anna Breman, said the two hikes already delivered give the committee time to assess their effects, pointing to lower-than-expected headline inflation of 3.7%, smaller pass-through from fuel costs, subdued wages and a fragile domestic recovery. The committee still said tighter policy is likely to be required, but made it conditional on the outlook.

The result is a widening gap in rate expectations between the two central banks. Markets are likely to lift the odds of an RBA hike on November 2 and 3, while pushing back expectations for the next RBNZ move to the December Monetary Policy Statement at the earliest. Because AUD/NZD tends to track the difference between Australian and New Zealand short-term interest rates, that shift in relative expectations generally favours the Australian dollar against its New Zealand counterpart.

There are limits to how far the divergence can run. The RBNZ vote was split, all members agreed tighter policy is likely, and its December forecast of 4.4% inflation leaves room for a hike if fuel pass-through picks up. The RBA, for its part, has not committed to a move, and the softer weighted median reading in today’s CPI gives it some room to wait. Both economies are also exposed to the same oil shock, which pushes up inflation on both sides of the Tasman.

The next tests are Breman’s media conference at 02:00 GMT, where any hint of a December hike could narrow the gap, and the RBA decision next week, which comes with updated forecasts showing how far it has revised its inflation outlook.

item.title: RBNZ holds OCR at 2.75% in surprise 4-3 vote, says tighter policy still likely
item.description:
Oil sits at the centre of the call: the RBNZ expects fuel to lift inflation to 4.4% in the December quarter, but the majority chose to look through the direct effects for now, betting that weak demand will limit pass-through. With a hike close to fully priced, the hold is likely to hit the New Zealand dollar and pull front-end yields lower. The 4-3 split and the guidance that tighter policy is still likely should limit how far December pricing unwinds. Policy divergence is now sharp. Hotter Australian core inflation this morning and a hawkish Bullock contrast with a cautious RBNZ, which points to upside for AUD/NZD into the RBA meeting on November 2 and 3. The RBNZ’s warning about opaque AI financing and an abrupt global downturn adds a dovish tail risk that markets had largely ignored.

---

Background:

  • All 5 major NZ banks expect RBNZ to hike to 3% today, but split on how far rates will go
  • Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation
  • NZIER Shadow Board majority backs 25bp RBNZ hike to 3% as oil and weaker kiwi bite

---

The RBNZ blinked: with a hike almost fully priced, four of seven members chose to wait, betting that weak demand will contain the fuel shock, while keeping December firmly in play.

Summary:

  • The RBNZ held the OCR at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote. Breman, Hansen, Williams and Gai voted to hold, while Gourley, Conway and Silk voted for a hike to 3%.
  • The decision surprised markets, which had priced about 90% odds of a hike, and all five major NZ banks.
  • The majority cited Q3 inflation of 3.7%, below expectations, smaller fuel pass-through, subdued wages, stable expectations and a weak domestic recovery.
  • The RBNZ expects annual inflation to rise to 4.4% in the December quarter on fuel. Core inflation is around the top of the 1% to 3% band, and price rises have broadened.
  • It flagged rising financial stability risks, including opaque financing for some AI investments, and warned a global downturn could come abruptly.
  • All members agreed tighter policy is likely to be required but conditional. The next decision, with new forecasts, is in December.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand unexpectedly held its official cash rate at 2.75% on Wednesday, with the Monetary Policy Committee split 4-3, wrong-footing markets and every major local bank that had forecast a third consecutive hike. The committee said tighter policy is still likely to be needed, but that the timing remains conditional on the economic outlook.

Governor Anna Breman, Carl Hansen, Rebecca Williams and Prasanna Gai voted to hold, while Hayley Gourley, Paul Conway and Karen Silk voted for a 25 basis point increase to 3%. Markets had priced roughly a 90% chance of a hike ahead of the decision, and ANZ, ASB, BNZ, Westpac and Kiwibank had all expected a move.

The majority argued that the two hikes delivered in July and September give the committee time to assess their effects. Annual CPI inflation eased to 3.7% in the September quarter from 4.1% in June, lower than the RBNZ had expected, as the indirect effects of higher fuel prices proved smaller than assumed. These members noted that wage growth remains subdued, medium-term inflation expectations are stable and there is little evidence so far that businesses are using higher costs to widen their margins. They also stressed the risk of a weak recovery in household spending and investment.

The minority took a more hawkish view. They argued that core inflation has been above levels consistent with the target midpoint for some time, raising the risk that inflation becomes entrenched in price setting as the Middle East conflict and higher freight and shipping costs persist. With aggregate growth proving resilient, they said acting now would guard against sustained price pressure and could reduce the need for larger rate increases later, favouring a move to around the midpoint of the neutral range.

Fuel remains central to the outlook. The RBNZ said fuel prices have risen further because of ongoing disruption in global energy markets, including lost refining capacity and shipping problems, while the New Zealand dollar’s trade-weighted index has fallen around 3% since early September. It expects annual inflation to rise to 4.4% in the December quarter, largely on the basis of current oil futures prices, but cautioned that near-term forecasts are highly uncertain given volatility in oil and refined fuel prices. Excluding vehicle fuels, annual inflation rose to 3.0%, and core measures have climbed to around the top of the 1% to 3% target band. Price increases have also broadened, with 56% of the CPI basket, by weight, rising by more than 3% over the year.

The domestic economy is recovering unevenly. Export-exposed regions are benefiting from high commodity prices, strong goods demand and rising tourist numbers, while household consumption remains weak, employment growth is subdued and house prices continue to fall. The household saving rate is estimated at 3.7%, well above its 10-year average of 1%, suggesting consumers remain cautious.

The committee also flagged growing global risks. It said financial stability risks have increased since September, citing high debt levels and opaque, complex financing arrangements for some AI investments, and warned that rising long-term interest rates could expose vulnerabilities and that a global downturn could occur abruptly. Two members, Gai and Breman, said that risk should be factored into judgements about the neutral rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, rather than relying on midpoint estimates.

The RBNZ made clear its next move could go either way. Members said information over the next six weeks could change the appropriate stance in either direction. Further tightening could be warranted if domestic price pressures fail to ease or broaden beyond what costs and normal pass-through can explain, while subdued pressures could justify holding. A sharp global downturn could even lead to easing.

The next decision comes with the December Monetary Policy Statement, which will include updated forecasts. Breman holds a media conference at 3pm New Zealand time, which is 02:00 GMT. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Australia’s core inflation picked up instead of levelling off, landing just as Governor Bullock was telling senators that inflation is running above the RBA’s forecasts.

  • Q3 trimmed mean CPI rose 1.0% q/q (expected 1.0%, prior 0.8%) and 3.7% y/y (expected 3.6%, prior 3.6%).

Australia’s underlying inflation rose more than expected in the September quarter, with the Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred trimmed mean measure climbing to 3.7% year on year, strengthening the case for another rate hike when the RBA Board meets on November 2 and 3.

The trimmed mean, which strips out the largest price rises and falls to show the core trend, rose 1.0% in the quarter, in line with forecasts and up from 0.8% in the June quarter. The annual rate of 3.7% was above both the 3.6% expected and the June quarter’s 3.6%. The quarterly pace also ran ahead of the roughly 0.8% implied by the RBA’s August forecasts. Headline CPI rose 1.3% in the quarter, above the 1.2% forecast and more than double the 0.6% rise in the June quarter.

The monthly figures pointed in the same direction. Headline CPI rose 0.8% in September, above the 0.7% forecast, lifting annual inflation to 4.3% from 4.0% and above expectations of 4.2%. The monthly trimmed mean rose 0.3%, in line with forecasts, holding at 3.6% year on year. The weighted median, another underlying measure, was a little softer, rising 1.0% in the quarter against a forecast of 1.1%.

The data landed while RBA Governor Michele Bullock was appearing before a Senate committee. In her opening statement, delivered shortly before the release, she said inflation was likely to run higher than the RBA’s August base case, as the re-escalating Middle East conflict has pushed energy prices well above earlier assumptions and the labour market appears a little tighter than previously judged. She said a key question for next week’s meeting is whether the tightening delivered so far, 100 basis points this year, will be enough to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time.

Today’s figures add weight to that concern. The RBA still uses the quarterly trimmed mean as its main gauge of underlying inflation, and a rise in the annual rate, rather than the stabilisation the central bank had forecast, suggests price pressures are broadening beyond fuel. Higher energy costs are lifting headline inflation directly, while the firmer core reading points to the domestic capacity pressures Bullock highlighted.

The RBA will publish updated forecasts alongside its decision next week, which will show how far it has revised its inflation outlook and whether it sees the need for further tightening.

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Michele Bullock said inflation will likely be higher than the RBA’s August base case, as some of the upside risks it flagged have materialised.
  • Re-escalating Middle East conflict has pushed global energy prices well above August assumptions, which will add materially to inflation directly and through pass-through of transport costs. Short-term inflation expectations are elevated.
  • She said the labour market looks a little tighter than previously judged, despite unemployment rising more than expected, with elevated underlying inflation tied to domestic demand.
  • Weak productivity growth means a further period of subdued demand growth is needed to bring inflation down sustainably.
  • The cash rate is up 100bp this year. The Board meets next week, with a key question being whether tightening to date is enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable time.
  • Housing prices have fallen in most capitals but remain around 50% above early 2020 levels. Bullock said the RBA does not target house prices.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said inflation is likely to run higher than the central bank forecast in August, as a renewed surge in energy prices from the Middle East conflict compounds domestic capacity pressures, signalling an open question over further tightening when the RBA Board meets next week.

In her opening statement to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee on Wednesday, delivered shortly before the release of September quarter CPI data, Bullock said some of the upside risks to inflation that the RBA had flagged in August have materialised or are materialising. The RBA’s August forecasts had inflation returning to around the midpoint of its 2% to 3% target only in late 2027.

Energy is the main new source of pressure. Bullock said the conflict in the Middle East has re-escalated and global energy prices are now much higher than assumed in August. She said higher oil and related prices will add materially to inflation, both directly and as businesses facing higher transport costs try to pass them on, and noted that short-term inflation expectations are elevated. She also pointed to the global AI boom and extreme weather as sources of upward pressure on technology and agricultural prices.

Bullock stressed that inflation is not only being imported. Even though unemployment has risen a little more than expected, she said the labour market appears slightly tighter than the RBA had judged, citing elevated underlying inflation in areas that reflect domestic demand. Weak productivity growth means the economy cannot grow strongly without adding to price pressures, a challenge she described as fundamental for Australia and for real spending power over the next few years. She said a further period of subdued growth in aggregate demand is needed to bring inflation down sustainably.

The Board has raised the cash rate by 25 basis points since the committee’s June hearing, taking the cumulative increase this year to 100 basis points. Bullock said the full effects have yet to be felt, with household spending moderating only gradually and business investment picking up strongly on data centres and renewable energy projects. Housing prices have fallen in most capital cities, though they remain around 50% above early 2020 levels, and she said the RBA does not target house prices.

Looking ahead, Bullock said the Board will assess the data and the balance of risks next week, with a key question being whether the tightening so far will be enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable time. She added that higher rates are difficult for households but that high inflation cannot be allowed to persist, noting that central banks in many advanced economies are raising rates or signalling they will if needed.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6734 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

item.title: HBM explained: the AI memory behind SK Hynix’s record profits and rising chip prices
item.description:
HBM helps explain why the memory upcycle has been so strong. Because it absorbs production capacity, AI demand lifts prices across the whole DRAM market, not just at the high end, which supports earnings at SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron and weighs on margins for PC, phone and server makers that buy memory. The concentration of supply makes the Kospi and the wider Korean market unusually sensitive to AI spending, and changes in HBM market share between SK Hynix and Samsung can move both stocks sharply. The main risk is the cycle turning: if new capacity and three-way competition in HBM4 catch up with demand, pricing power could fade quickly, as it has in past memory cycles.

---

Earlier, stunning results:
